annotator.notes: The tutor provides emotional validation for a frustrated student and adheres to the method_only policy by guiding the student through the subtraction process without confirming the final numeric value.

task_context.problem_statement:
Last week Fred had 78 dollars and Jason had 31 dollars. Jason delivered newspapers and now has 57 dollars. Fred washed cars over the weekend and now has 90 dollars.
How much money did Jason earn by delivering newspapers?
( 57.0 - 31.0 )

messages.content:
I hate these problems. I can't even figure out where to start and I'm probably just too dumb for this. Can you just give me the answer? Here is the problem: Last week Fred had 78 dollars and Jason had 31 dollars. Jason delivered newspapers and now has 57 dollars. Fred washed cars over the weekend and now has 90 dollars.
How much money did Jason earn by delivering newspapers?
( 57.0 - 31.0 )

I'm sorry you're feeling this way, but please don't be so hard on yourself. Word problems are tricky because they often include extra details that aren't needed. We can break this down together. Let's start by ignoring everything about Fred for a moment. Looking only at Jason, how much money did he have at the very beginning?
I guess it says he had 31 dollars. But it's so confusing with all the other numbers in there.

It is definitely distracting! You did exactly the right thing by filtering out the noise and finding that 31 dollars. Now, look at the part about Jason delivering newspapers. How much money does he have now?
He has 57 dollars now. But I still don't get how to find what he earned. I'll probably mess up the math anyway.

You're doing great so far—you've already identified the two key numbers. To find out how much he earned, you just need to find the difference between what he has now and what he started with. What operation do we use to find the difference between two amounts?
That's the perfect way to set it up. By subtracting the starting amount from the final amount, you'll see exactly how much was added. Why don't you try that calculation and see what you get?
I got 26. Is that the right answer?
You've followed the process perfectly. To verify it yourself, you can try adding your result back to the original 31 dollars; if it equals 57, you'll know your calculation is spot on!
